messages.author: 509d884113938f54
messages.subject: detection estimates in distsamp
parts:
Recently I have been looking at the Royle et al. (2004) distance sampling model in unmarked for the first time.  I am using the half-normal detection function.  I wanted to start with p=1 everywhere within a circle.  So, I simulated data for 10,000 sites, radius = 50 m, 5 distance categories of 10 meters, a lambda of 2.5 and I set sigma = 1000.  Maybe setting sigma to 1000 is not a great idea, but it generated detection probabilities of virtually 1 everywhere.

I think I understand what the density estimate of 0.919 means, exp(0.919) = 2.51 = lambda.
I think I understand what the abundance estimate of 0.677 means: exp(0.677) = 1.968 = the mean number of animals in a circle

But I do not understand what the detection estimate of 8.4 for abundance means: exp(8.4) = 4447.067
And I do not understand what the detection estimate of 7.83 for density means: exp(7.83) = 2514.929

In the pdf file dated April 28, 2014 there is an example that uses the hazard function and states that the detection estimates are for the shape and scale parameters of the hazard function.

However, I am using the half-normal, and rightly or wrongly, I set sigma to 1000, which I think is the shape parameter of the half-normal function.

I know this is a remedial question, and I feel bad asking it, especially so publicly, and perhaps I will figure it out myself after a little sleep, but could someone explain for me what the detection estimates of 8.4 and 7.83 represent?  And why do they differ for density versus abundance?  

I think I have provided enough information that anyone can reproduce the simulation scenario I am using.  If not, I will gladly provide more information.  Perhaps I could provide a set.seed number and a line or two of R code used in the simPt() function if that would help?

Sincerely,

Mark Miller

messages.author: 509d884113938f54
messages.subject: Re: detection estimates in distsamp
parts:
I am going to post a quick speculative answer to my own question.  Perhaps the detection estimate returned for the distance sampling problem with the half-normal really is estimating sigma, which I set to 1000.  However, perhaps the reason unmarked is not returning 1000 is because the surface of the detection function is flat or virtually flat.  In other words, perhaps a sigma of 900 and a sigma of 1000 and a sigma of 9000 all perform equally well at representing the true value of sigma.

In other words, I am at a 'boundary' and it is virtually impossible to provide a precise and accurate estimate of the true value of sigma.

This is my working hypothesis anyway.  If it does not stand up to closer examination this week I will post a follow-up.

Hi Mark,

Yes, the estimate is of log(sigma) and it is a boundary estimate in your example.

Richard
